title: ArchPHI
oneLiner: ArchPHI is building the operating system for architectural drawings. The first product reads CAD drawings and writes the bill of quantities — the list of materials and work a builder has to price.
summary: Architects deliver their designs as CAD files. ArchPHI reads those files and writes the bill of quantities. One rule sits under everything: the system only states facts it can point to in the drawing. When the drawing has no answer, it says so instead of guessing. It is tested on eight real projects.
role: Founder & CTO. I build the system. My cofounder is the licensed professional who checks the results.
privateNote: The test projects are real client work. They stay anonymous. Drawings, quantities, and bills stay private.
problem: Real CAD files are messy. Some parts are corrupt. Some point to files that were never delivered. Some dimensions show a typed-in number that is different from the drawn length. Software that guesses over files like these gives confident wrong answers, and in construction wrong numbers cost real money. So the base layer has one job: make it impossible for a guess to look like a fact.
constraints: Every office draws differently. The system has to learn words like door and window from each project's own drawings, because a built-in list would fail on the next office.
A corrupt drawing has to show up in the results as a broken file. Dropping it quietly would hide missing work.
The common CAD format (DWG) cannot be read directly. Files are converted first, and each conversion is recorded, because converting can lose detail.
AI calls cost money. Every call gets a price and a spending cap before it is allowed to run.

approach.decision: No building-element names in the code. A check runs on every build and fails it if a word like door or window appears in the core code.
approach.why: Hardcoding one office's names makes the system fail on the next office. A failing build cannot be ignored.

approach.decision: Read the drawing's real geometry instead of screenshots of it.
approach.why: The CAD file holds exact lines, text, and measurements. Every extracted fact keeps an ID, so it can be checked again later.

approach.decision: Count everything once. One pass over all eight projects counted 2,668,953 drawing records and put each one in exactly one bucket: readable, partly readable, or unsupported.
approach.why: The count shows exactly what the system can and cannot read. It also states its own limit: readable here does not mean understood.

approach.decision: Score against hidden answer sheets. The system gets a bill with blanks to fill. The answer sheet is never shown to it. Every line lands in one of six buckets, such as correct, wrong, or flagged as unknown.
approach.why: The system cannot score well by guessing, and it cannot hide behind saying I do not know. Seventeen scored runs are saved.

approach.decision: Delete work that fails its own test.
approach.why: An earlier pipeline could not read 12 of 16 real sheets, so it was removed. A staged preparation step scored worse than a plain control, 16 against 22 of 39 lines, so it was never merged.

implementation: A reader that turns CAD files into exact geometry, with a record of where every piece came from.
An intake step that classifies every delivered file and records each DWG-to-DXF conversion. Broken files are kept and marked as broken.
A check for missing references. One sheet pointed to 21 images that were never delivered. All 21 were flagged.
Dimension reading from real geometry. All 766 readable dimensions gave a supported measured value. 13 had typed-over text, and each one was flagged.
The scoring harness with hidden answer sheets, with 17 runs saved.
A diagnosis of the biggest open failure, area measurement: 1 of 14 lines correct over 42 tries.

outcomes.label: drawing records counted across eight projects, each in exactly one bucket
readable dimensions gave a supported measured value
a plain control beat the staged pipeline on a 39-line bill, so the pipeline was not merged

limitations: 74.1% of records handled does not mean 74.1% of a drawing understood.
There is no product accuracy number yet. The scoring system exists to earn one.
The takeoff product is not shipped. First firms are onboarding soon.
Area measurement does not work yet: 1 of 14 lines correct over 42 tries. The drawings do not carry the height the calculation needs.

title: PiloneCables
category: Website for a cable factory · pilonecables.com
oneLiner: Pilone makes electrical cable in Pakistan. I built and run their website. In six months, clicks from Google grew from 204 to 1,070 and the average search position moved from 17.8 to 8.4.
summary: The site has 288 pages: product pages, guides, and calculators, all generated from the factory's own data. The numbers on this page come from Google Search Console, which is Google's own report of how a site performs in search.

featuredMetric.label: clicks from Google, six months against the six before

metrics.label: average position in Google results over the same window
times shown inside AI search answers, in three months
pages on the site: 96 products, 89 guides, 70 city pages, plus tools

problem: Buyers search Google for cable types, sizes, and prices, and they found the big brands. Pilone's site had about 65 pages in Google and no answers to those searches.
constraints: Prices and specifications change, so the pages are generated from the factory's data.
Many weak pages hurt ranking. Every page has to answer a real search or be removed.
People now ask AI assistants instead of Google, so the site has to be readable for AI crawlers too.

approach.decision: Generate the pages from factory data.
approach.why: Buyers search for exact products and sizes. The factory's own data answers those searches, and competitors cannot copy data they do not have.

approach.decision: Delete weak pages. The pipeline once generated 1,053 pages. 405 thin ones were deleted and 236 became redirects. 288 stayed.
approach.why: Google ranks a site better when every page has a clear answer. The rankings improved after the deletion.

approach.decision: Build calculators buyers actually use: cable size and voltage drop.
approach.why: A calculator answers a question a table cannot, and its use is a sign of buying intent.

approach.decision: Make the site readable for AI search.
approach.why: Three months later the site had been shown 3,870 times inside AI answers, up from zero.

approach.decision: Check Search Console and let the numbers pick the next task.
approach.why: Position and clicks decide what to build next.

implementation: A static site where every page is generated from factory data at build time.
A build pipeline that syncs prices and rebuilds navigation, the search index, and the sitemap.
Cable-size and voltage-drop calculators, plus reference charts.
Search across all pages, on the page itself.
Analytics with events for contact clicks and calculator use.

outcomes.label: clicks from Google, six months against the six before
times shown inside AI search answers, three months

limitations: Times shown in results grew from 9.92k to 46.2k, but part of that window had a known Google logging error. Clicks and position are the numbers I trust.
Pages on the site and pages Google has indexed are different counts.
There was no controlled experiment. The evidence is the before and the after.

title: TalentFlow
oneLiner: A recruitment platform built at a research lab. It gathers a candidate's public information, matches it to jobs by meaning, and runs the first interview with a voice agent. Four engineers built it. I led the team.
summary: Instead of matching CVs by keywords, the platform turns text into embeddings. An embedding is a list of numbers that captures meaning, so texts that mean similar things get similar numbers. Candidates and jobs land in the same number space, and close means a good match. On top of that, a voice agent runs the first interview: it picks a topic, asks a question out loud, listens to the answer, and continues. At the end it writes a scored report.
role: Team lead. Four engineers, and I owned the architecture.
privateNote: Built over personal data inside a lab. Described by how it works, never by candidates.
problem: Recruiters skim CVs and miss what is on a candidate's GitHub or personal site. The lab wanted the whole first pass automated: gather the information, match it to a role, and run a first interview.
constraints: Five sources with five different formats — CV, GitHub, LinkedIn, a research registry, personal sites — all with personal data.
Lab servers only, so everything had to be self-hosted and easy to rebuild.
The interview must never repeat a question, and answers have to come fast enough to feel like a conversation.
Small open models only.

approach.decision: Match by meaning instead of keywords.
approach.why: Two texts can say the same thing with different words. Embeddings still match them.

approach.decision: Rewrite job ads before matching them.
approach.why: Job ads are short and messy. A cleaned and expanded version matches candidates better.

approach.decision: Build the interviewer as a loop of small parts.
approach.why: One part remembers what was asked. One part picks the next topic. One part writes the question. Splitting them is what stops repeated questions.

approach.decision: Run the model on Groq, a service that runs open models very fast.
approach.why: A conversation feels wrong when answers come slowly.

approach.decision: Split the system into services in Docker containers.
approach.why: Each stage runs at its own pace, and the whole system can be rebuilt on lab servers with one command.

implementation: Ingestion that gathers and cleans candidate data from all five sources.
Matching on embeddings stored in a vector database, a database that finds items by similarity.
The interview loop: pick a topic, write a question, speak it, transcribe the answer, continue.
A report step that runs at the end and scores the session.
The services deployed with Docker on lab servers.

outcomes.label: Led the four-engineer team and owned the architecture
The agent answers in under five seconds and does not repeat questions, as observed during development

limitations: Match quality was never measured. There is no number that says the matching works better.
The under-five-seconds figure was observed during development.
It is a lab prototype. Before real candidates it would need consent, data retention rules, and access controls.

title: Revvy
oneLiner: Revvy reads a business's Google reviews and writes reply drafts. A person approves each reply before it posts. Built for a client, running on the Simplabots platform.
summary: Revvy connects to Google Business Profile, the system behind a business's Google listing and its reviews. It pulls the reviews in, drafts a reply for each one in the business's voice, and a person approves or edits it before it posts. Each business chooses how much runs on its own: nothing, drafts only, or auto-posting for good reviews. Revvy runs as an agent on the Simplabots platform.
privateNote: Built for a client. No business names, accounts, or review text are shown anywhere.
problem: A business with many locations gets more reviews than anyone can answer. Automating it the naive way is slow and wasteful: pulling thousands of reviews one at a time takes over an hour, and drafting a reply for every single review spends AI money on reviews that need none.
constraints: Real customer data under Google's rules. Nothing identifying leaves the system.
Google access expires while a long sync runs, and access can also be revoked for good. The code has to tell those two apart.
Every AI call costs money, and Google limits how fast you can call its API.
Many businesses on one system, kept fully separate.

approach.decision: Filter first, draft second.
approach.why: Reviews that are already answered, or below the chosen star rating, never reach the AI. That cut drafting cost by about a third to a half.

approach.decision: Three drafting modes instead of one.
approach.why: Small batches run fast in parallel. Large backfills run overnight at about half the cost. A slowed-down mode stays inside Google's speed limits.

approach.decision: Handle Google access properly.
approach.why: Access is refreshed before it expires, and a revoked account is marked as needing reconnection instead of being retried forever.

approach.decision: Keep the background job queue inside the database.
approach.why: One less system to install, watch, and debug.

approach.decision: Write to the database in batches.
approach.why: A full sync used to make about 2,000 small writes. Batching cut that to a few dozen. Syncing 2,000 reviews went from one to two hours down to 10 to 20 minutes.

implementation: The Google connection, including access that survives long syncs.
Review ingestion that pulls pages of reviews and saves them in batches.
The drafting step, with a per-location voice and settings.
The three modes: manual, draft then approve, and auto-post above a chosen star rating.
Background jobs for syncing, drafting, and posting.
The dashboard: connect, see locations, and approve or edit drafts.
limitations: The speed numbers come from the project's own benchmark notes.
Reply voice comes from written instructions per location. A memory of past replies is prepared but switched off.
I would want checks on reply quality before trusting auto-posting more widely.

title: Emmy
oneLiner: Emmy sorts a business inbox. It labels every email inside Gmail itself and keeps a note of why. Built for a client, running on the Simplabots platform.
summary: Emmy sorts incoming mail into the client's own categories and applies each decision as a normal Gmail label. Known senders are sorted by fixed rules and never cost an AI call. Everything else goes to the AI, which reads the whole conversation before deciding. Every decision is saved with its reason and can be checked in a dashboard.
privateNote: Runs on real client inboxes. How it works is public. What is in the inbox is not.
problem: A client wanted incoming mail sorted into their own categories, inside the inbox they already use. Sending every email to an AI is slow and expensive, and it can put two emails from the same conversation into different folders. Simple rules alone cannot handle the mail that needs judgment. And when the system sorts something wrong, correcting it has to teach it.
constraints: New mail has to be labeled quickly, or the sorting is useless.
Email content never leaves the server.
Known senders must never cost an AI call.
A conversation has to stay in one category.
Corrections have to change future behavior without retraining anything.

approach.decision: Two layers: fixed rules first, AI second.
approach.why: Most mail comes from known senders. A sender list sorts those instantly and for free. The AI only sees the mail that actually needs judgment.

approach.decision: Sort conversations instead of single emails.
approach.why: The AI reads the whole conversation, and moving one email moves the thread. Mail from one conversation landing in two folders is the mistake people notice first.

approach.decision: Give the AI clear facts and demand a fixed answer format.
approach.why: The AI sees who sent it, whether the client was addressed directly or copied in, and what each category means. If the answer does not fit the format, the email is left unsorted instead of guessed.

approach.decision: Feed corrections back in.
approach.why: The last ten corrections are shown to the AI when it decides. The client's habits show up in the sorting within days, with nothing to retrain.

approach.decision: Let the client's contact groups drive the sorting.
approach.why: The client already knows who their senders are. Groups can be filled from a simple file upload, and each group routes to its categories automatically.

implementation: The path from Gmail to the sorter: new mail triggers a background job that sorts in small batches.
The rules layer that matches senders and domains to contact groups.
The AI step with its fixed answer format and safe fallback.
Label writing, including putting everything back in the inbox if the account is removed.
The saved reason for every decision, shown in the dashboard.
The dashboard: categories, contact groups with file upload, a setup wizard, and a conversation view.

outcomes.label: Known senders are sorted instantly, at zero AI cost
Every decision is stored with its reason and can be checked in the dashboard
Live as an agent on the Simplabots platform

limitations: The confidence score is a simple flag. It marks the cases where the AI fell back to a default.
Some mail is left unsorted on purpose. For genuinely unclear mail, a person deciding is the right outcome.
A similarity-search layer is wired into the database but switched off. I would measure whether it helps before using it.

title: MelodyMind
oneLiner: A music app from my thesis. Describe a situation — a breakup, a rainy drive, a late night of studying — and it finds songs that fit it. It takes text, a picture, or your voice.
summary: Most music search matches a mood word like sad or happy. That was never the goal. A sad song about a breakup is not a sad song about losing someone, and the app should hear that difference. To compare a described situation with actual audio, both are turned into embeddings — lists of numbers that capture meaning — in one shared space. The design that worked: a pretrained audio embedding model called CLAP, kept frozen, with one small trained layer that maps songs into the same space as the text.
role: Built with Hassaan Anwar and Saad Nadeem. I set up the backend and built the voice DJ end to end — speech to text, text to speech, and the session logic — plus the chat system and the first Spotify integration.
problem: Ask for a song for a breakup, and the request is words while the answer is sound. A mood tag cannot carry the difference between two situations that share a mood. Our first attempts showed how hard the problem is: mood classifiers over lyrics and image-style networks over audio both collapsed, and every song came out with nearly the same numbers.
constraints: No dataset links situations to songs. The training pairs had to be built from public sources.
Only short public audio previews were available, not full tracks.
No budget to train an audio model, so the design had to reuse a pretrained one.

approach.decision: Keep the pretrained audio embedding model (CLAP) frozen and train one small layer on top.
approach.why: CLAP already turns audio into useful numbers. Training one small layer to map those numbers into the text space needs little data and little computing power.

approach.decision: Train that layer by pulling matching pairs together and pushing everything else apart. The method is called InfoNCE.
approach.why: It teaches two things at once: match a song to its description, and keep different songs apart. The second part is what fixed the collapse.

approach.decision: Test the pretrained model first, with ten situation prompts.
approach.why: It handled clear emotions and tempo well but missed situations like a focus session. That gap is what the trained layer had to close.

approach.decision: Build the training data from places where people already describe music in real situations: Reddit threads, Last.fm tags, and lyrics, paired with audio previews.
approach.why: People describing music to each other is the closest thing to situation-to-song data that exists.

approach.decision: Build playlists with vector math.
approach.why: Once songs and situations share one space, a playlist is the songs closest to the request. Simple to build and simple to inspect.

implementation: The trained layer that maps audio embeddings into the text space.
The data pipeline over Reddit, Last.fm, lyrics, and audio previews.
The backend and the vector search that builds playlists.
The voice DJ: you speak, it transcribes, updates the playlist, and answers out loud.
Picture-to-playlist: the app reads the situation in a photo and searches with it.
A tool that splits a song into vocals, drums, bass, and the rest.
The mobile app, tested on real phones.

outcomes.label: Training became stable after 17 full passes over the data, with clear separation between songs
A working prototype on real phones: playlists from text, pictures, and voice
Song splitting shipped in the final iteration, with downloadable tracks

limitations: Playlist quality was never measured against a benchmark.
It is a research prototype, not a launched app.
